catalog_quote: Like most Nigerian languages, Gbari is a tone language and every vowel can have one of five possible tones. There are three level tones and two glides, rising and falling. The glide tones are rare and they could be analysed as combinations of level tones. However, they seem to occur in isolation on some words which indicates that they must be treated as separate tonemes. new_statements.rule_in_words: Gbari is described purely as a lexical tone language (H, M, L level tones plus rare rising and falling contours, tone-bearing syllabic nasals); none of the accessible first-hand descriptions (Blench & Doma; Alerechi & Chiemezie 2019 on the Kwali dialect; Blench 1989/2013) says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: glide tones rare, possibly decomposable into level sequences; Gbari shows downdrift but (per Blench 2013) not terraced tone; Adeniyi & Elugbe 2018 describe downstep for (Kuta) Gwari.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on citation forms of the Sumwakpna (Kwali-area) lect; no word- or phrase-level prominence is discussed. Alerechi & Chiemezie 2019 (p.219, Kwali dialect, own fieldwork) independently state 'Gbari, like most African languages, is a tonal language' with three basic tones, likewise with no stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench & Doma's dictionary describes the Sumwakpna lect near Kwali (southern Gbari / Gbari-Yamma) and Alerechi & Chiemezie 2019 the Kwali dialect; both fall under Gbari gbar1246 (Glottolog dialect 'Gbagyi Nkwa' gbag1257 is listed under gbar1246). Hyman & Magaji 1970 and Adeniyi & Elugbe 2018 describe Kuta Gwari, i.e. Gbagyi (East Gwari, ISO gbr, gbag1258), the sister language; H. Rosendall 1992 covers both clusters.
